title: AST Function Extraction — Core Method
description: Rather than regexing source text, the inspector parses code into an abstract syntax tree and reads the structure directly: every function and class definition with its name, arguments, and line numbers. AST parsing understands scope, nesting, and decorators, which text search cannot. The extraction also captures docstrings, giving a one-line summary per callable. This is how IDEs and documentation generators see code, and it is the only reliable way to inventory a program. At ladder rank 1 this is the simple core: a single, self-contained application of the method.
demo:
import ast
src = "def add(a, b):\n    \"\"\"Add two numbers.\"\"\"\n    return a + b\n"
tree = ast.parse(src)
for node in ast.walk(tree):
    if isinstance(node, ast.FunctionDef):
        args = [a.arg for a in node.args.args]
        print("function %s(%s) line %d" % (node.name, ", ".join(args), node.lineno))

title: Import Inventory — Core Method
description: A program's dependencies start with its imports, and the inspector lists every imported module with the names actually used. Standard-library imports are separated from third-party ones, because the two have very different installation stories. Unused imports are flagged as cleanup candidates, and dynamic imports are noted as harder to analyze. The import inventory is the first page of any dependency or security review. At ladder rank 1 this is the simple core: a single, self-contained application of the method.

title: Entry-Point Detection — Core Method
description: To run a program you must know where it starts: the inspector finds main() functions, __main__ guards, console-script declarations, and top-level executable statements. Each candidate entry point is reported with how it is invoked — 'python module.py' versus 'import then call'. Ambiguous cases, like scripts that do work at import time, are flagged as risky to import. Knowing the entry points turns an inert code archive into runnable software. At ladder rank 1 this is the simple core: a single, self-contained application of the method.

title: Complexity Scoring — Core Method
description: Cyclomatic complexity counts the decision points — ifs, loops, boolean operators — in each function, and high scores mark code that is hard to test and risky to change. The inspector scores every function and ranks them, so reviewers start where the risk is. The metric is simple enough to compute from the AST in one pass, yet it correlates well with real defect rates. Complexity reports guide refactoring budgets toward the functions that need them most. At ladder rank 1 this is the simple core: a single, self-contained application of the method.
demo:
import ast
src = "def f(x):\n    if x:\n        for i in range(x):\n            if i > 2: return i\n    return 0\n"
tree = ast.parse(src)
decisions = sum(1 for n in ast.walk(tree)
                if isinstance(n, (ast.If, ast.For, ast.While, ast.BoolOp)))
print("decision points:", decisions, "-> complexity", decisions + 1)

title: Signature Inventory — Core Method
description: The signature inventory lists every public callable with its full signature — parameter names, defaults, and annotations — forming the program's API surface at a glance. Private helpers are separated from the public API by naming convention. Changes to this inventory between versions reveal breaking API changes automatically. For an archive of programs, the signature inventory is the catalog that lets users find code they can actually call. At ladder rank 1 this is the simple core: a single, self-contained application of the method.
